catalog_quote: A light syllable has one mora and a heavy syllable has two moras as in (2.11). [...] Recall that Lynch (2000) assigns stress to the penult syllable if the final vowel is short, or to the ultima if it contains a long vowel or a vowel cluster. So, maunu ‘rain’ and lolo ‘sink’ have penultimate stress because they have a final short vowel, i.e. a mono-moraic ultima. The words babai ‘hot’ and rufuː ‘my village’ have ultimate stress because their nuclei are bi-moraic. A heavy syllable always receives stress, because a prosodic foot in the language is built from either one heavy syllable or two light syllables. [...] The Wuvulu prosodic foot is a trochee consisting of two moras. A moraic trochee in Wuvulu is built counting moras right-to-left from the right edge of the word. A foot can consist of either one heavy syllable (σH) or two light syllables (σL) as in (2.12). [...] Stress falls on the head of the trochee. In (2.13)b. the foot is built from a heavy syllable, and the ultima is considered to be extrametrical [...] Words are right-headed, meaning that cumulative, primary stress falls on the right-most trochee of the word, and with secondary stress, if present, falling on the second trochee from the right edge of the world.
world_status: statement found in an open source

All three quoted segments are there verbatim, in order, with the report's [..] marking the elided material: "So, maunu 'rain' and lolo 'sink' have penultimate stress because they have a final short vowel, i.e. a mono-moraic ultima. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the head of the rightmost moraic trochee, built right-to-left: on the penultimate syllable when the final syllable is light (short vowel), and on the final syllable when it is heavy (long vowel or diphthong). Heavy syllables always attract stress; long vowels always bear word stress. Equivalently (Lynch 2000, as quoted by Hafford): penult if the final vowel is short, final if it is long or a vowel cluster. Surface final stress in forms like [gufú] 'my kinsman' is the result of suffixation (/kufu-u/) and rightward stress shift (Blust 1996, 2008).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress, if present, falls on the second trochee from the right edge (Hafford 2015:34, e.g. manumanu 'something', ʔaiʔolu '1PL.EXCL'; [ˌna.ʔu.ˈpo.lu] 'highlander' p. 42). Blust 1996:16 records quadrisyllables with secondary stress on the initial syllable and primary on the penult.
new_statements.exceptions: Blust 1996:16 found primary stress 'optionally on the initial or the penultimate syllable of trisyllabic bases' (e.g. [bíLoLo]~[biLóLo] 'butterfly') and one suggested but doubtful minimal pair (afelo 'rotten (of wood)' vs 'bad'); Hafford 2012 §3 says 'a few exceptions appear' to the moraic-trochee account. Stress is explicitly non-contrastive (Blust 1996:15–16; Blust 2013 §4.1.10).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level. At phrase level the first of two juxtaposed NPs gets its final vowel lengthened and hence ultima stress (Hafford 2015:24, 34, §3.1), which distinguishes NP juxtaposition from compounds (compounds keep penultimate primary stress). Phrasal intonation described separately (§2.3.4).
new_statements.identity_note: Hafford 2015 describes Wuvulu proper (Glottolog dialect wuvu1240; Onne village ~75% of data, Auna ~25%), not the Aua dialect (auaa1241); Blust 1996:16 covers both and states 'The stress rules of Aua are essentially identical to those of Wuvulu', and Lynch 2000 (as quoted) gives the same rule for Seimat, Wuvulu and Aua. Hafford 2012 uses Onne-dialect surface forms.

new_statements.quote: Languages in this category have only open syllables, and assign primary stress to the penultimate syllable if the final vowel is short, or to the final syllable if its vowel is long or if it contains a vowel cluster. The extant languages of the Western Admiralty family, Seimat, Wuvulu, and Aua (Blust 1996), fall into this category. Blust says of Wuvulu and Aua that primary stress in fact falls optionally on the initial or the penultimate syllable of trisyllabic bases, but on the penult in others (Blust 1996:16). Surface final-syllable stress derives from an underlying penultimate geminate vowel cluster: for example, /kufu/ [gúfu] 'island' vs. /kufu-u/ [gufú] 'my kinsman'. [p. 61] ... The languages of the Western Admiralties assign primary stress on the basis of right-aligned moraic trochees (see 3.2.2). [p. 64]

new_statements.relation_note: Same rule as the catalog's 'weight' record and Hafford 2015's existing statement (penult if final vowel short, ultima if long/vowel-cluster; moraic trochees). Hafford 2015:33 quotes exactly this Lynch passage and builds his moraic analysis on it, so the agreement is by descent, not independent. Lynch additionally reports Blust 1996's optional initial stress in trisyllables, a detail the catalog does not carry.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Wuvulu (with Seimat and Aua) has only open syllables; primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable when the final vowel is short, and on the final syllable when the final vowel is long or is a vowel cluster (i.e. a heavy final syllable). Lynch restates this as right-aligned moraic trochees with primary stress on the rightmost foot; final-syllable stress arises from an underlying penultimate geminate (kufu-u 'my kinsman' [gufú]). Lynch adds, from Blust 1996:16, that in trisyllabic bases primary stress falls optionally on the initial or the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing specific to Wuvulu. The paper's abstract quotes Ross (1998:18) for the general Oceanic pattern of secondary stress on every second syllable before the penult, and Lynch's POc reconstruction is a right-aligned moraic-trochee system, but no Wuvulu secondary-stress facts are given.
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllabic bases: stress 'optionally on the initial or the penultimate syllable' (reported from Blust 1996:16). No other exceptions for Wuvulu; the survey material is second-hand (Blust 1996), and Lynch's own conclusion section says his proposal 'must remain tentative until such time as we have better data on stress in these languages' (p. 80), directed mainly at the Eastern Admiralties.
new_statements.identity_note: Lynch groups Wuvulu with Seimat and Aua as 'the extant languages of the Western Admiralty family' and states the rule for all three together, following Blust 1996; the trisyllable remark is attributed to 'Wuvulu and Aua'. No dialect is singled out.

new_statements.quote: Like most Austronesian languages of the Pacific Islands, stress is usually penultimate for Wuvulu words. For words of four or more syllables, stress typically occurs penultimate within each of the two-syllable parts of the word (i.e., stress iterates backwards on even-numbered syllables preceding the primary stress). There are several grammatical environments which cause stress to fall on the ultima. These involve a lengthened word-final vowel and are discussed in the section on morphophonemics. [...] [6.1] There are four grammatically determined environments in which a word-final vowel is lengthened in duration, resulting in what sounds to be a stressed ultima.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Hafford 2015 statement (penult by default, ultima when the final nucleus is bimoraic/long): agrees on type and placement, and adds the leftward-iterating secondary stress and the list of morphological environments that create long final vowels. One difference of detail: here diphthongs are said to pattern as single vowels for stress ([»bai.bai] 'mosquito' with initial stress), whereas Hafford 2015 treats a final diphthong as bimoraic and stress-attracting (babai 'hot' with final stress); the 2005 transcriptions themselves are mixed ([na.»nao], [«fa./o.»bao] final-stressed). The catalog record (world-r2-2026-09-17) has an empty rule, so nothing there to contrad…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default primary stress on the penultimate syllable; when a word-final vowel is lengthened (a geminate/bimoraic final vowel, arising in listed morphological environments) stress falls on the ultima, e.g. [»hu.mu] 'house' vs [hu.»muu] 'my house', [»ha.xo] 'spouse' vs [ha.»xoo] (possessed). The author refers the reader to Kenstowicz on moraic association and syllable weighting, i.e. a right-aligned quantity-sensitive trochee. Diphthongs are said to 'pattern as single vowels for syllabification and stress' (e.g. [»/ai.poi], [»bai.bai], [»mau.nu]), though some transcriptions show final stress on a final diphthong ([na.»nao], [«fa./o.»bao]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: In words of four or more syllables stress 'iterates backwards on even-numbered syllables preceding the primary stress', i.e. secondary stress on alternate syllables leftward from the primary: [«fai.na.»xo.a] 'eight', [«ma.fu.»fu.o] 'morning', [«pu.nE.»ha.fi] 'coral stove'; with a lengthened final vowel the secondary stays in place: [«na.xa.»na.xa] 'thought' vs [«na.xa.na.»xaa] 'thinker' (p. 103).
new_statements.exceptions: Ultimate stress in five morphologically determined environments where the final vowel is lengthened (6.1.1-6.1.5): transitive verb before an explicit object NP ([«bi.gi.»/aa]), head noun of a juxtaposed possessed-possessor NP ([ha.»xoo]), 1sg possessive -u on u-final nouns ([hu.»muu]), reciprocal fi-..-i on i-final words ([fi.ta.»fii]), attributive -a on a-final nouns ([«na.xa.na.»xaa]). Also optional final-vowel drop after a nasal (hu.»mu.mu -> hu.»mum) and a respectful greeting register with lowered pitch and lengthened stressed syllable (5.3).
new_statements.identity_note: Hafford 2005 states the data were collected on Wuvulu Island over nine years and 'are therefore not representative of the Aua dialect'; the two Wuvulu-Island dialects differ only in one conditioned allophone and a slight intonation difference. The 2004 sheet is headed Wuvulu-Aua [WUV] and mentions the Auna village dialect (Wuvulu Island) and Aua [r] for /x/, but its stress statement is not dialect-specific.

new_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress is nearly always penultimate for words of less than four syllables. For two-syllable words that are reduplicated, stress occurs penultimate within each of the two-syllable parts of the word.

On its own this is fixed: penultimate syllable (hedged 'nearly always'); as a bar…
new_statements.relation_note: A two-sentence OPD sheet by the same author: it states only the penultimate default ('nearly always'), which is the default placement in the existing Hafford 2015 weight-sensitive statement and in Hafford 2005; it is silent on the heavy/long-final-vowel ultimate stress, so it is coarser rather than contradictory. Read on its own it would be classed fixed: penultimate syllable; the fuller works by the same author identify the 'nearly always' residue as bimoraic finals.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is (nearly always) on the penultimate syllable in words of up to three syllables; in reduplicated disyllables each half carries penultimate stress. The sheet says nothing about vowel length, syllable weight, final long vowels or tone (no tone is reported; the heading is the standard OPD template).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only the remark that reduplicated two-syllable words have stress on the penult of each two-syllable part (i.e. a secondary stress on the first half); no general statement.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'nearly always' without naming the exceptions; separately notes optional dropping of a final high front vowel (aipani 'five' -> aipan) with conditions not yet determined.
new_statements.identity_note: Hafford 2005 states the data were collected on Wuvulu Island over nine years and 'are therefore not representative of the Aua dialect'; the two Wuvulu-Island dialects differ only in one conditioned allophone and a slight intonation difference. The 2004 sheet is headed Wuvulu-Aua [WUV] and mentions the Auna village dialect (Wuvulu Island) and Aua [r] for /x/, but its stress statement is not dialect-specific.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: all three Hafford sources (2004 OPD sheet, 2005 OPD supplement, 2015 dissertation already in existing_statements) give penultimate stress as the default, and the two fuller ones (2005, 2015) put stress on the ultima when the final vowel is long/bimoraic, with the 2005 supplement listing the morphological environments that create such long final vowels and adding alternating secondary stress leftward. The only difference of detail is the treatment of diphthongs: Hafford 2005 says diphthongs pattern as single vowels for stress (e.g. [»bai.bai] 'mosquito'), while Hafford 2015 counts a final diphthong as a bimoraic, stress-attracting nucleus (babai 'hot' with final stress); the 2005 transcriptions are themselves inconsistent on this point ([na.»nao], [«fa./o.»bao] with final stress). The 2004 sheet's bare 'nearly always penultimate' is a coarser statement, not a competing analysis.

sources.note: 'stress appears a priori to be contrastive in Wuvulu and Lindrou, but in both cases it is better explained in other ways. Wuvulu shows phonetic contrasts such as [gúfu] 'island' : [gufú] 'kinsman', but closer attention to morphology shows that the latter is /kufu-u/ 'my kinsman', and a rule of rightward stress shift together with the contraction of morphologically-derived sequences of identical vowels accounts for the surface contrasts.' (secondary, summarising Blust 1996)
